history.heading: Medieval and Ottoman Kosovo
paragraphs: The region of Kosovo has been inhabited since ancient times, by Illyrian and Dardanian peoples, and later became part of the Roman and Byzantine empires. Slavs arrived in the 6th and 7th centuries. In the Middle Ages, Kosovo was the heart of the Serbian kingdom and home to important Orthodox monasteries, such as Gračanica, Visoki Dečani and the Patriarchate of Peć, now UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

The Battle of Kosovo in 1389 between Serbian-led forces and the Ottomans became a central event in Serbian national memory. Kosovo was part of the Ottoman Empire for over 500 years, during which many Albanians, who became the majority, converted to Islam. The League of Prizren, founded there in 1878, was a key moment in the Albanian national movement.

history.heading: Yugoslavia and war
paragraphs: Serbia took control of Kosovo in 1912. In Yugoslavia, Kosovo became an autonomous province in 1974. In 1989 Serbian leader Slobodan Milošević revoked its autonomy, and Albanians were dismissed from jobs and public life; they created parallel institutions under Ibrahim Rugova's peaceful resistance.

An armed insurgency by the Kosovo Liberation Army began in the late 1990s. Serbian forces responded with brutal repression and mass expulsions of Albanians. In 1999 NATO bombed Serbia for 78 days, after which Serbian forces withdrew and Kosovo came under UN administration. Many Serbs and Roma then left.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: Kosovo declared independence from Serbia on 17 February 2008. The International Court of Justice ruled in 2010 that the declaration did not violate international law. Kosovo is recognised by around half of UN member states, including the United States and most EU countries, but not by Serbia, Russia, China or five EU members.

culture.heading: Peoples and traditions
paragraphs: Over 90 percent of the population is ethnic Albanian; Serbs are the largest minority, mainly in the north and in enclaves, along with Bosniaks, Turks, Roma and others. Albanian and Serbian are official languages. Most Albanians are Muslim, with Catholic minorities, while Serbs are Orthodox.

Kosovo has a young population and a vibrant cultural scene, including the Dokufest documentary festival in Prizren. Singers Dua Lipa and Rita Ora have Kosovo-Albanian roots. Flija, a layered pancake dish, is a traditional food.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Kosovo is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the government, and parliament elects the president; 20 seats are reserved for minorities. Vetëvendosje (Self-Determination), led by Albin Kurti, has been the largest party since 2019.

Normalising relations with Serbia through EU-led dialogue is the central issue; tensions in the Serb-majority north have flared repeatedly. A NATO-led peacekeeping force (KFOR) remains. Kosovo has applied for EU membership, and its citizens gained visa-free travel to the Schengen area in 2024.

economy.heading: Developing economy
paragraphs: Kosovo is one of the poorest economies in Europe, though growth has been steady. Remittances from the large diaspora in Germany, Switzerland and elsewhere are vital. Key sectors include construction, trade, services and IT outsourcing. Kosovo has large reserves of lignite, used for electricity.
Kosovo uses the euro, though it is not part of the eurozone. Unemployment, especially among young people, and emigration are major challenges.
